answers.answer: An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata (status and headers) for reuse. A browser private cache serves that user agent; a CDN runs shared caches at edge servers near users; origin is the server responsible for the resource. A hit reuses a suitable stored response, and a miss lacks a usable response. Empty caches: browser → CDN → origin, then response origin → CDN → browser; each cache stores only if policy permits. A browser hit answers locally without a network request. Another browser that misses locally can get a CDN hit, avoiding origin. These are stored HTTP responses, not replicated database records; origin may consult a database, but hits need not reach it. Request hit ratio is hits divided by requests at a specified layer: CDN 800/1000 = 80%, with 200 origin requests under the stated assumptions. Browser hits never reached this denominator. Sizes differ, so this is not byte hit ratio or bytes saved; real validation, background refreshes, extra layers and application/database work require separate measurement. Repeated public assets and popular pages can lower latency through nearby responses and reduce origin requests and transfer. CDN requests/transfer can cost money, and key configuration, invalidation and monitoring cost operational work. For low-traffic mostly private or rarely reused Notes responses, compare measured reuse, latency and total cost and omit shared caching when benefits do not justify costs; keep privacy rules intact.

evidence.quote: An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata, such as status and headers, for reuse.
With empty caches, the request goes browser → CDN → origin.
A browser hit avoids the network request. After a browser miss, a CDN hit avoids origin.
The ratio is 800 / 1,000 = 80%.
Browser hits never entered that denominator.
For a low-traffic application serving mostly private or rarely reused responses, omit shared caching if measured benefits do not justify those costs.

answers.answer: Cache-Control carries response caching rules. public explicitly permits shared caching subject to other rules; max-age=60 sets a 60-second freshness lifetime; s-maxage=300 overrides it only for shared caches. Fresh means young enough to reuse without validation under policy; stale means its freshness limit has been reached, not necessarily that its body was deleted. Age estimates seconds since generation or successful origin validation, including time in caches. At Age 90 the browser has zero fresh time left (60−90 = −30: 30 seconds stale), while the CDN is fresh with 300−90 = 210 seconds left. Delivery does not restart lifetime and freshness does not prove origin content is unchanged. A representation is a returned resource form. Revalidation checks whether the stored representation is still usable; ETag is its opaque validator, preserved without interpretation. The stale CDN sends a conditional GET to origin with If-None-Match: "v1", requesting a body only if the selected representation no longer matches. If unchanged, origin returns 304 Not Modified without a replacement body; CDN updates applicable metadata including freshness and serves its retained v1 body for the ordinary browser GET. If changed, origin returns 200 with the new v2 body and validator (ETag: "v2"); CDN replaces the stored representation if allowed and serves the new body. The lesson does not specify particular new freshness header values for either response. ETags do not push changes into other caches. A 304 saves body transfer across the validation hop but still requires an origin round trip and may involve application or database work.

evidence.quote: Freshness is permission to reuse, not proof that origin content is unchanged.
The CDN has 300 − 90 = 210 seconds of freshness left.
Receiving it does not start a new full lifetime.
ETag is an opaque validator identifying that representation; clients preserve the tag rather than interpreting it.
If unchanged, origin returns 304 Not Modified without a replacement body.
The CDN updates applicable stored metadata, including freshness information, and uses its retained body to answer the browser's ordinary GET.
Origin was still contacted and may run application logic or query a database to decide whether the representation changed.

answers.answer: Cookies are browser-held state: Set-Cookie asks the browser to store it and Cookie sends it back. Authorization is a request header carrying credentials. Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks resource-access permission. For the public page choose unqualified no-cache: storage is allowed but every reuse requires successful validation. For a private note whose browser storage is acceptable choose private: shared-cache storage is forbidden, browser storage is allowed subject to other directives, and private alone does not require validation on every use. For sensitive notes choose no-store: HTTP caches must not store the response, but this does not erase delivered copies or replace permission checks. Cookie and Set-Cookie neither automatically produce per-user entries nor universally prevent caching. Authorization requests have special shared-cache restrictions, yet response policy can permit reuse, so authentication alone is not a universal bypass guarantee. Reusing one user's shared response for another can leak private notes. Keep authorization at origin, explicitly set private/no-store as appropriate, verify actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse for private routes, and test different users. Do not make personalized responses public to raise hit ratio.

evidence.quote: Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permission to access a resource.
For a public page, unqualified no-cache allows storage but requires successful validation before every reuse.
For a sensitive response, no-store instructs HTTP caches not to store the response.
Cookie and Set-Cookie do not automatically create per-user cache entries or universally prevent caching.
For private routes, verify that explicit private/no-store policies and actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse.

answers.answer: A cache key identifies the stored response that can satisfy a request. HTTP caching uses method and target URL plus selected request headers to distinguish variants, which are different returned forms of a resource. Keep ?format=pdf distinct from ?format=html, and keep Accept-Language en distinct from fr. Vary identifies request-header distinctions needed for matching: Vary: Accept-Language requires that header value to match for reuse when supported and honored. If the CDN ignores query parameters, verify and correct its actual matching configuration so format and language both survive; bypass caching until they do. Dropping format can return HTML for a PDF request, and losing language separation can match the wrong language. Irrelevant tracking parameters create extra entries and fewer hits; exclude only those confirmed not to change the response. Vary does not change the URL, grant permission, or override private/no-store. It never authorizes sharing private notes.

evidence.quote: A cache key identifies which stored response can satisfy a request.
Vary: Accept-Language tells a cache that this request header's value must match for reuse.
verify that both format and language survive the actual matching rules, or bypass caching until they do.
Exclude them only after confirming they do not change the response.
Vary does not change the URL, grant permission or override private/no-store.

answers.answer: A versioned asset URL changes when the bytes change. Publish changed JavaScript as app.v2.js instead of overwriting app.v1.js; immutable bytes at each URL suit long caching. Update the referring page to request v2, while an old cached page can still request v1. For a mutable published page that keeps its URL, choose freshness/revalidation to match the tolerated update delay, such as short freshness or validation on each reuse. A database edit does not rewrite cached HTTP responses. A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries according to the provider. Verify relevant URL, variant and CDN-layer coverage, propagation and completion behavior; it is not guaranteed simultaneous replacement everywhere. A purge does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloads. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges, but cannot instantly revoke already delivered public content. Choose lifetimes with that limit in mind.

evidence.quote: A versioned asset URL changes when its bytes change: publish app.v2.js instead of overwriting app.v1.js.
Update the referring page to request v2; an old cached page can still ask for v1.
A database edit does not rewrite stored HTTP responses.
Verify coverage of the relevant URLs, variants and CDN cache layers, plus propagation and completion behavior.
Purging CDN entries does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloaded content.

answers.answer: stale-while-revalidate allows bounded stale reuse while attempting background validation, hiding its latency. stale-if-error allows bounded stale fallback on eligible errors such as origin failure. These permissions are optional, not freshness or availability guarantees. Freshness expires at age 60; stale allowances start then. At age 75 the response is 15 seconds stale and inside the extra 30-second window (through age 90), so it may be served while attempting background validation. At age 150 it is 90 seconds stale; with an eligible origin error it is within the 120-second error allowance (through age 180), so fallback is permitted. At age 200 it is 140 seconds stale: both extensions are exhausted and these directives no longer permit stale reuse. A cold cache has no copy to fall back to, and expired allowances can expose failure. Verify support and policy; the directives do not override private/no-store. Private-data correctness and urgent removal may forbid using an old copy even if stale serving helps public-help availability.

evidence.quote: stale-if-error permits bounded stale fallback on eligible errors, such as an origin failure.
The response is fresh for 60 seconds; stale windows start when freshness expires.
At age 200 neither extension still permits stale reuse.
A cold cache has no response to fall back to, and exhausted allowances can expose the failure.
Private-data correctness or urgent removal may forbid stale reuse even when it improves public-help availability.
